note:
Nurse: Triage summary for the doctor. This is a 69-year-old female with known polymyalgia rheumatica who came in with worsening shoulder and hip pain. Blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 84, temperature 98.4 F, oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Doctor: Thank you. Good afternoon. I understand the pain has come back. Tell me what has been going on.

Patient: It feels just like last year. My shoulders and hips are so stiff in the morning that I can barely get out of bed. It lasts about two hours, and I can't lift my arms to comb my hair. It started about ten days ago.

Doctor: Last year you were diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica and started on prednisone. What dose are you taking now?

Patient: Prednisone, 5 mg once a day, I think. I was tapering because my rheumatologist said I was doing so well.

Doctor: Okay, 5 mg. When did you last lower it?

Patient: About two weeks ago, and the pain started soon after. I have also been taking ibuprofen, 400 mg twice a day, just to get through the days.

Doctor: I see. Any headache, jaw pain when you chew, or vision changes?

Patient: No headache, no jaw pain, and my vision is fine. No fever either.

Doctor: Any rash, black stools, or stomach pain with the ibuprofen?

Patient: No rash, no black stools, and no stomach pain. It is the muscles. They ache and feel heavy.

Doctor: What other conditions do you have, and what else do you take?

Patient: I have high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and thin bones. I take lisinopril 20 mg once a day, metformin 1000 mg twice a day, alendronate 70 mg once a week, omeprazole 20 mg once a day, and calcium with vitamin D.

Doctor: Thank you. Let me examine you. Lifting your arms out to the side hurts and stops at about shoulder height, and lifting your knee against my hand is painful at the hip. There is no joint swelling in your hands, wrists, or knees, and no temporal artery tenderness. Your labs came back while we were talking. The ESR is 58 and the CRP is 31 mg/L, hemoglobin is 12.1, creatinine is 0.9, and your blood sugar is 196.

Patient: Wait, I need to fix something. My daughter just sent me a photo of my bottle, and it says 7.5 mg, not 5. I went down from 10 mg to 7.5 mg two weeks ago.

Doctor: Thank you for checking. So your current dose is 7.5 mg once a day, and the pain began right after that drop. My impression is a flare of polymyalgia rheumatica from tapering too quickly. Giant cell arteritis is unlikely because you have no headache, jaw pain, or vision changes. I am going to increase your prednisone back up to 10 mg once a day. I also want you to stop the ibuprofen, because with prednisone it raises the risk of a stomach bleed. Use acetaminophen if you need something for pain. Keep taking your other medicines the same, and check your sugars twice a day while the steroid dose is higher.

Patient: That makes sense. The problem is getting to the rheumatology clinic. I do not drive, and my neighbor takes me only when she can.

Doctor: I understand. We will do a telephone visit with the rheumatology team in one week instead of asking you to travel. You can have the ESR and CRP repeated at the lab near your home in two weeks, and our staff will set up a ride through your insurance transportation benefit for the next in-person visit. Please call or come back right away if you get a headache, jaw pain, or any change in your vision.

Patient: I will. Thank you, doctor.
summary: A 69-year-old female with known polymyalgia rheumatica presented to urgent care with ten days of morning stiffness and aching in the shoulders and hips that began after her prednisone was lowered to 7.5 mg once a day. She denied headache, jaw pain, vision changes, and fever, and had no joint swelling or temporal artery tenderness, while the ESR was 58 and the CRP 31 mg/L. The assessment was a polymyalgia rheumatica flare after a taper that was too fast. Prednisone was increased to 10 mg once a day and ibuprofen was stopped. Because transportation makes clinic visits difficult, follow-up will be by telephone with repeat labs near home.

soap.subjective: 69-year-old female with known polymyalgia rheumatica presenting with worsening shoulder and hip pain for about ten days, with morning stiffness lasting about two hours and difficulty lifting her arms. Symptoms began soon after she lowered prednisone from 10 mg to 7.5 mg once a day two weeks ago (she first reported 5 mg, then corrected the dose from her bottle). She has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg twice a day. Denies headache, jaw pain, vision changes, fever, rash, black stools, and stomach pain. History of high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and thin bones; takes lisinopril 20 mg once a day, metformin 1000 mg twice a day, alendronate 70 mg once a week, omeprazole 20 mg once a day, and calcium with vitamin D. Transportation to the rheumatology clinic is difficult because she does not drive and relies on a neighbor.
soap.objective: BP 138/82, heart rate 84, temperature 98.4 F, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Active arm elevation limited by pain at about shoulder height and painful hip flexion against resistance; no joint swelling in the hands, wrists, or knees; no temporal artery tenderness. ESR 58, CRP 31 mg/L, hemoglobin 12.1, creatinine 0.9, blood sugar 196.
soap.assessment: Flare of polymyalgia rheumatica after a prednisone taper that was too rapid. Giant cell arteritis is considered unlikely given no headache, jaw pain, or vision changes.
plan: Increase prednisone to 10 mg once a day
Stop ibuprofen because of the stomach bleeding risk with prednisone; acetaminophen if needed for pain
Continue other medicines unchanged
Check blood sugars twice a day while the steroid dose is higher
Telephone visit with the rheumatology team in one week instead of travel
Repeat ESR and CRP at a lab near home in two weeks
Arrange a ride through the insurance transportation benefit for the next in-person visit
Call or return right away for headache, jaw pain, or any change in vision

note:
This is a follow-up visit for a 59-year-old male with stable exertional angina. He reports chest pressure when he walks briskly uphill or climbs two flights of stairs. The pressure lasts about three minutes and resolves with rest. The frequency is about twice a week and has not changed over the past three months. He denies pain at rest, syncope, palpitations, and orthopnea. He has used sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg as needed only once in the past month, with prompt relief.

His history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Current medications are metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, and nitroglycerin 0.4 mg as needed. He reports taking all of them reliably.

On examination, blood pressure was 136/84, heart rate 62, respiratory rate 14, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Heart rhythm was regular with no murmurs. There was no JVD and no peripheral edema, and the lungs were clear. A resting ECG showed sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute with no ST changes. A treadmill stress test last month reproduced his typical chest pressure at stage 3 with 1.5 mm of horizontal ST depression and no arrhythmia. His recent lipid panel showed an LDL of 92 mg/dL.

My impression is stable exertional angina with an abnormal stress test, hypertension that is above goal, and an LDL that is not at goal for his risk. I increased atorvastatin from 40 mg to 80 mg daily and started amlodipine 5 mg daily to improve both angina control and blood pressure. He will continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, and nitroglycerin as needed. I ordered coronary CT angiography to define his anatomy, and we will repeat the lipid panel in eight weeks. I reviewed warning signs, and he should go to the emergency department for chest pain at rest or lasting longer than fifteen minutes despite nitroglycerin. He will return in six weeks.
summary: A 59-year-old male with stable exertional angina reported chest pressure about twice a week with brisk uphill walking or two flights of stairs, relieved by rest and unchanged for three months. He denied pain at rest, syncope, palpitations, and orthopnea. Blood pressure was 136/84, a treadmill stress test reproduced his chest pressure with 1.5 mm of ST depression, and LDL was 92 mg/dL. Atorvastatin was increased to 80 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily was started. Coronary CT angiography was ordered, with a repeat lipid panel in eight weeks and return in six weeks.

Start amlodipine 5 mg daily for angina control and blood pressure
Continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, and nitroglycerin as needed

Return in six weeks

note:
This is a dictation for a follow-up visit in the oncology clinic for a 66-year-old female with stage one invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, estrogen receptor positive, progesterone receptor positive, HER2 negative, status post lumpectomy and whole breast radiation, now fourteen months into adjuvant anastrozole. She came in anxious and had a long list of questions written on a notepad. History of present illness, she tells me she has been taking the anastrozole only twice a week, correction, every other day, for about the last three months because the copay went up and she is trying to stretch the bottle, and she had not told anyone until today. She also reports aching and stiffness in both hands and both knees that is worse in the morning, which she attributes to the medicine, and she has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg twice a day for it. She denies a new breast lump, nipple discharge, bone pain, cough, shortness of breath, headache, abdominal pain, and weight loss.

Past medical history includes hypertension and hypothyroidism. Medications are anastrozole 1 mg once daily as prescribed, amlodipine 5 mg once daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg once daily, calcium with vitamin D, and the ibuprofen I mentioned. She has no known drug allergies.

On exam blood pressure is 154/92, heart rate 78, and weight is stable at 164 pounds. She looks anxious but is in no distress. Breasts are symmetric with a healed lumpectomy scar on the left without nodularity, and there is no axillary adenopathy bilaterally. Lungs are clear and the abdomen is soft and nontender. There is no bony tenderness over the spine. Labs this week, CBC with hemoglobin 12.8, WBC 5.6, platelets 232, creatinine 0.9, and TSH 2.1. Her diagnostic mammogram six months ago showed no evidence of recurrence. A DEXA scan this month shows a lumbar spine T-score of minus 2.6, which is osteoporosis.

During the visit she asked many questions. She asked whether skipping doses raises the chance the cancer returns, and I explained that missed doses reduce the benefit of the treatment so taking it every day matters. She asked whether she should switch to tamoxifen, and I explained that it is an option if the aromatase inhibitor cannot be tolerated, but that her joint symptoms may be partly treatable and we should first fix the cost problem. She asked whether the joint pain means the cancer has spread, and I told her that is very unlikely given the normal exam, the normal labs, and the pattern of the pain. She asked whether she needs more scans, and I said no routine scans are needed beyond her yearly mammogram.

For the assessment, one, hormone receptor positive invasive ductal carcinoma on adjuvant anastrozole with partial adherence because of cost. Two, aromatase inhibitor arthralgias. Three, osteoporosis. Four, hypertension above goal. Five, hypothyroidism, stable. For the plan, continue anastrozole 1 mg once daily and take every dose, and I referred her to our financial counselor and pharmacy to apply for manufacturer assistance and to move to the lowest cost generic. Stop ibuprofen because it can raise blood pressure, and start acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for joint pain. Start alendronate 70 mg once weekly and continue calcium with vitamin D, and a dental check is advised before long-term alendronate. Increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg once daily, with a home blood pressure log. Repeat the mammogram in six months, follow up with me in eight weeks, and she can call the nurse line with any questions between visits.
summary: A 66-year-old female with hormone receptor positive invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, fourteen months into adjuvant anastrozole, came in anxious with many questions after taking the medication only every other day for three months because of cost. She reported aching and stiffness in her hands and knees and denied a new breast lump, bone pain, and weight loss. Blood pressure was 154/92 and a DEXA scan showed osteoporosis. The assessment included aromatase inhibitor arthralgias, osteoporosis, hypertension above goal, and stable hypothyroidism. Anastrozole was continued with financial counseling, alendronate and acetaminophen were started, ibuprofen was stopped, and amlodipine was increased to 10 mg once daily.

note:
Telehealth note, telephone visit (audio only). The patient is a 65-year-old female with persistent asthma who called in for worsening control over the past 3 weeks. She has nighttime cough and wheezing about 3 nights a week and now uses her albuterol inhaler about 4 times a week, up from once a week. She also gets short of breath climbing one flight of stairs. She denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, and colored sputum. Home peak flow this morning was 270 L/min, below her personal best of 380 L/min, and her home pulse oximeter reading was 96%. She takes fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 mcg, one inhalation twice daily, and reports missing no doses. She has no other chronic conditions.

No physical exam was possible by telephone. She spoke in full sentences during the call.

Impression: poorly controlled persistent asthma. Recommendations: increase fluticasone-salmeterol to 500/50 mcg, one inhalation twice daily, and continue albuterol as needed. I reviewed inhaler technique by phone, and she described a slow deep inhalation with a breath hold. She should rinse her mouth after each use. We will schedule spirometry at an in-person visit in 4 weeks and a follow-up call in 2 weeks. She should go to urgent care or call 911 if her peak flow drops below 190 L/min, if she needs albuterol more often than every 4 hours, or if she cannot speak in full sentences.
summary: A 65-year-old female with persistent asthma had a telephone visit for 3 weeks of worsening control, with nighttime cough and wheezing about 3 nights a week and albuterol use about 4 times a week. She denied fever, chest pain, leg swelling, and colored sputum, and her home peak flow was 270 L/min against a personal best of 380 L/min. No exam was possible by telephone. The impression was poorly controlled persistent asthma. Fluticasone-salmeterol was increased to 500/50 mcg twice daily, with spirometry planned and a follow-up call in 2 weeks.

Spirometry at an in-person visit in 4 weeks

note:
Telehealth note, video visit. The patient is a 62-year-old female seeking evaluation of gradual hearing loss. Her daughter, who lives with her, joined the video call and provided part of the history. Over about 2 years, the patient has noticed trouble following conversation in restaurants and when several people talk at once. Her daughter reports that she turns the television volume up and often asks people to repeat themselves. The loss seems about the same in both ears and has not changed suddenly. She denies ear pain, ear drainage, dizziness, and tinnitus. She has not had recent ear infections or head injury. Her only chronic condition is hypertension, and she takes lisinopril 10 mg once daily.

On video, her external ears looked normal, with no visible drainage. She had to ask me to repeat questions when I spoke at a normal volume with my face turned away, but understood me well when I faced the camera and spoke slowly. Otoscopy and a hearing test cannot be done by video.

Impression: gradual, probably bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, most consistent with presbycusis. Recommendations: in-person visit for otoscopy and audiometry, and a hearing aid evaluation if the audiometry confirms hearing loss. In the meantime, face her when speaking and reduce background noise. She should call sooner for sudden hearing loss, ear pain, or dizziness.
summary: A 62-year-old female was seen by video for about 2 years of gradual hearing loss, with her daughter providing part of the history. She turns the television volume up and has trouble following conversation in noisy settings, and she denied ear pain, ear drainage, dizziness, and tinnitus. On video her external ears looked normal and she understood better when facing the camera. The impression was probable bilateral sensorineural hearing loss consistent with presbycusis. An in-person visit for otoscopy and audiometry was recommended, with a hearing aid evaluation if hearing loss is confirmed.

Otoscopy and hearing test not possible by video.

Hearing aid evaluation if audiometry confirms hearing loss
Face her when speaking and reduce background noise
Call sooner for sudden hearing loss, ear pain, or dizziness

note:
Telehealth note, video visit. The patient is an 81-year-old female with chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes, here for a scheduled nephrology follow-up. She joined from home using her tablet and could hear and speak clearly. She reports mild fatigue over the past month and knee pain from osteoarthritis that she has been treating with over-the-counter ibuprofen about twice a day. She denies shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, and decreased urine output. She has had no recent falls or poor oral intake.

Home measurements she took before the visit were blood pressure 132/76, heart rate 70, and weight 142 pounds, unchanged from her last visit. On video she appeared comfortable and spoke in full sentences, and no leg swelling was visible on camera.

Current medications are losartan 50 mg once daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and acetaminophen 500 mg as needed. Labs drawn last week showed creatinine 1.5 and eGFR 36, which is stable compared with 3 months ago, potassium 4.9, hemoglobin 11.2, and a urine albumin-creatinine ratio of 180 mg/g.

Impression: chronic kidney disease stage 3b with moderately increased albuminuria, stable. Her eGFR is below the level where full-dose metformin is recommended, and ibuprofen is not safe for her kidneys. Her blood pressure is near goal.

Recommendations: reduce metformin to 500 mg twice daily. Stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for knee pain, not exceeding 3000 mg per day. Start dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily for kidney and cardiovascular protection, with instructions on hydration and sick-day rules. Continue losartan 50 mg once daily. Repeat a basic metabolic panel in 2 weeks after starting dapagliflozin, and repeat the urine albumin-creatinine ratio in 3 months. Follow-up video visit in 3 months, sooner if she develops vomiting, diarrhea, or poor oral intake.
summary: An 81-year-old female with chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes had a video nephrology follow-up and reported mild fatigue and knee pain treated with over-the-counter ibuprofen. She denied shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, and decreased urine output, and home blood pressure was 132/76. Creatinine was 1.5 and eGFR 36, which is stable. Metformin was reduced to 500 mg twice daily, ibuprofen was stopped, and dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily was started. A basic metabolic panel will be repeated in 2 weeks and follow-up is in 3 months.

note:
Hospitalist progress note, dictated on hospital day 3 for a 44-year-old male admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed. Overnight events, none. He had no further black tarry stools and no vomiting, and he denies chest pain, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness this morning. He was admitted with black tarry stools and one episode of coffee-ground emesis after about two weeks of burning epigastric pain. He had been taking ibuprofen 600 mg three times a day for low back pain. He works night shifts at a warehouse with a rotating schedule, which is why he went so long without seeing anyone and why his meals and sleep are irregular. He has no known drug allergies.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy on hospital day 1 showed a duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel, treated with epinephrine injection and hemoclip placement. A rapid urease test was positive for Helicobacter pylori. He received one unit of packed red blood cells for a hemoglobin of 7.6, and the most recent hemoglobin this morning is 8.2, correction, 8.4. BUN has improved to 18, creatinine 0.9, INR 1.0, and platelets 245.

Vitals this morning, blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 84, down from 112 on admission, temperature 98.2 F, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On exam he is comfortable, the abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no rebound, and there is no guarding. Stool is brown.

Assessment is upper gastrointestinal bleed from a duodenal ulcer related to NSAID use and Helicobacter pylori infection, with acute blood loss anemia, hemodynamically stable. The intravenous pantoprazole course is complete, so I am changing him to oral pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily. Ibuprofen is permanently discontinued and he was counseled to avoid all NSAIDs, and I started acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for back pain. I am starting Helicobacter pylori treatment with amoxicillin 1000 mg twice daily and clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily together with the pantoprazole for 14 days. Because his work hours rotate, I asked him to time doses to when he wakes and before his first meal rather than by the clock, and we set up a pill organizer and wrote the schedule on his discharge instructions. Diet advanced to regular. Repeat hemoglobin in the morning, and if stable he can be discharged tomorrow with a work excuse letter. He will follow up with gastroenterology in four weeks, and a test to confirm Helicobacter pylori eradication should be done at least four weeks after the antibiotics.
summary: A 44-year-old male on hospital day 3 of an upper gastrointestinal bleed from a duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel, treated endoscopically, had no further black tarry stools or vomiting. Hemoglobin was 8.4 after one unit of packed red blood cells, and the rapid urease test was positive for Helicobacter pylori. He was changed to oral pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily, ibuprofen was permanently stopped, and acetaminophen, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin were started. Dosing was tied to his waking time because he works rotating night shifts, and discharge is planned tomorrow if hemoglobin is stable.

Initially said onset 3 d ago -> corrected on further q: URI sx (sore throat, cough, low-grade temps) 3 d ago, CP started ~18 h PTA. NKDA.

note:
This is a dictation for a postpartum follow-up visit for a 34-year-old female, gravida 2 para 2, who is now three weeks after a primary cesarean delivery at term. Her course was complicated by readmission on postpartum day 6 with postpartum endometritis, and she was hospitalized for four days. She has a documented allergy to penicillin with hives, so she was treated with intravenous clindamycin and gentamicin instead. A pelvic ultrasound during that stay showed no retained products of conception, blood cultures were negative, and she went home after 48 hours without fever, with no antibiotics needed at discharge.

Today she reports she is feeling much better but very tired, which she attributes to broken sleep with the baby. She is breastfeeding with good latch and supply. Bleeding is light and has decreased to spotting. She denies fever, chills, foul-smelling lochia, headache, visual changes, chest pain, calf pain, and drainage from the incision.

She has chronic hypertension, hypothyroidism, and iron deficiency anemia. Medications are nifedipine ER 30 mg once daily, levothyroxine 88 mcg once daily, ferrous sulfate 325 mg, and a prenatal vitamin. She told me she takes the ferrous sulfate twice daily, correction, once daily, because the twice daily dosing upset her stomach. She stopped oxycodone 5 mg a week ago and now uses ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours as needed for incisional pain, which is compatible with breastfeeding. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 8, and she did not endorse thoughts of self-harm.

On exam blood pressure is 146/94, repeated at 142/92, heart rate 76, and temperature 98.2 F. The incision is well healed without erythema, induration, or drainage. The fundus is firm below the umbilicus. Lungs are clear. Urine dipstick is negative for protein. The CBC today shows hemoglobin 10.2, up from 9.1 at discharge, with white count 7.4 and platelets 310. A pelvic exam was deferred.

For the assessment, one, postpartum endometritis, resolved after treatment. Two, chronic hypertension, above goal postpartum. Three, iron deficiency anemia, improving. Four, hypothyroidism on treatment. For the plan, increase nifedipine ER from 30 mg to 60 mg once daily and keep a home blood pressure log twice daily, and call for readings of 160 over 110 or higher, severe headache, or visual changes. Stop ibuprofen because it can raise blood pressure, and use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed instead. Oxycodone remains discontinued. Continue ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily and repeat the CBC in four weeks. Continue levothyroxine 88 mcg once daily and check a TSH in six weeks. For contraception, estrogen-containing methods are not appropriate with her hypertension and breastfeeding, so I started norethindrone 0.35 mg once daily, and we discussed an intrauterine device as an alternative. Continue the prenatal vitamin and lactation support. She will return in three weeks for a blood pressure check and her comprehensive postpartum visit.

note:
Hospital day 2 progress note for a 25-year-old female admitted after a first unprovoked seizure. She had a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting about two minutes, followed by post-ictal confusion for roughly twenty minutes, and she sustained a tongue laceration. She had no preceding illness, head trauma, alcohol or drug use, or sleep deprivation, and has no prior history of seizures. There has been no seizure activity overnight. She reports a mild headache and soreness of the tongue this morning, and denies fever, neck stiffness, focal weakness, numbness, and vision changes. She has a history of migraine without aura and takes no regular medications other than an oral contraceptive.

Vital signs this morning: blood pressure 112/68, heart rate 72, respiratory rate 14, temperature 98.6 F, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. On examination she is alert and oriented, with a healing laceration on the lateral left side of the tongue. Cranial nerves, strength, sensation, reflexes, and gait are normal, and there is no meningismus.

Sodium 139, glucose 92, creatinine 0.7, and calcium and magnesium are normal. Urine drug screen is negative and urine pregnancy test is negative. CT of the head was normal on arrival. MRI brain with and without contrast showed no structural lesion. The EEG obtained yesterday showed intermittent left temporal sharp waves without clinical events.

Impression: first unprovoked seizure, with an abnormal EEG that raises the risk of recurrence enough to justify starting treatment. I started levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily yesterday, and she is tolerating it without sedation or mood change. Lorazepam 2 mg IV remains ordered as needed for a seizure lasting longer than five minutes. I counseled her on seizure precautions, no driving until cleared by neurology, avoiding alcohol and sleep deprivation, and avoiding swimming or bathing alone. We discussed that levetiracetam can cause irritability and she should report any mood change. Her oral contraceptive is not affected by levetiracetam. She will be discharged today with a prescription for levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, to be taken at the same times each day, and outpatient neurology follow-up in two weeks.

note:
Telehealth note, telephone visit (audio only), patient at home. The patient is a 56-year-old female with known Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum and colon who called with a 2-week history of worsening symptoms. She reports 6 to 8 loose stools per day, up from her baseline of 1 to 2, with crampy lower abdominal pain, urgency, and nighttime awakenings to use the toilet. She has had weight loss of about 5 pounds, from 153 to 148 pounds on her home scale. She also reports tiring easily. She denies blood in the stool, vomiting, fever, mouth sores, and new joint pain.

She was prescribed adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks. She admits she skipped her last two doses because the copay increased after her insurance plan changed and she could not afford it. She has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg a few times a day for the cramping.

Her home temperature this morning was 98.9 F. No physical examination was possible by telephone. Her voice sounded tired but she spoke in full sentences. Labs drawn last week at her local lab were reviewed: CRP 28 mg/L, hemoglobin 11.4, albumin 3.4, and fecal calprotectin 640 mcg/g.

Impression: Crohn's disease flare, precipitated by interruption of adalimumab because of cost, with mild anemia. Recommendations: order stool testing for Clostridioides difficile today, and she will drop off the sample at her local lab. Start prednisone 40 mg once daily once that test is negative, then taper by 5 mg each week, with calcium and vitamin D while on steroids. Stop ibuprofen because NSAIDs can worsen Crohn's disease, and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for cramping. Resume adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks. Our office will submit a prior authorization and a copay assistance application today and refer her to the clinic social worker for help with insurance costs, and the specialty pharmacy will deliver to her home. Repeat the CRP and CBC in 2 weeks, with a nurse call in 1 week to check on symptoms. She should go to the emergency department for fever, vomiting, severe abdominal pain, or blood in the stool.

note:
Hematology/Oncology consult note

Reason for consult: Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia with fever, evaluation of management and growth factor support. Requesting service: general medicine, hospital ward.

History of present illness: The patient is a 37-year-old male with stage III diffuse large B-cell lymphoma receiving R-CHOP, who presented to the emergency department last night with fever and chills. At home he measured a temperature of 101.9 F. He also reports mild mouth soreness. He denies cough, shortness of breath, dysuria, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. On intake he told the team that he received his last chemotherapy two weeks ago, correction, the oncology infusion record shows cycle 2 day 1 was nine days ago. Pegfilgrastim was not given after cycle 2 because it was not authorized in time. Blood cultures were drawn and he was started on cefepime on arrival.

Pertinent history: Hypertension, obesity, and GERD. He has a right chest implanted port placed before chemotherapy. He currently smokes about one pack of cigarettes per day for 15 years and drinks alcohol rarely. He takes several over-the-counter supplements started after his diagnosis: echinacea, turmeric capsules, and St. John's wort for mood. He first told us he had stopped the St. John's wort before chemotherapy, but on further questioning he clarified that he took it daily until admission.

Medications before admission: lisinopril 20 mg once daily, omeprazole 20 mg once daily, acyclovir 400 mg twice daily for prophylaxis, and ondansetron 8 mg every 8 hours as needed for nausea. No known drug allergies.

Examination: Tmax 101.9 F, blood pressure 108/64, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Ill-appearing but nontoxic. Mild oral mucositis on the buccal mucosa without thrush. The port site is without erythema, tenderness, or drainage. Lungs are clear and the heart is tachycardic and regular. The abdomen is soft and nontender. No rash.

Data review: WBC 0.6 with an absolute neutrophil count of 180, hemoglobin 9.8, platelets 88, creatinine 1.0. Chest x-ray shows no infiltrate. Urinalysis is negative. Blood cultures from the port and a peripheral vein have no growth at 18 hours.

Impression: One, chemotherapy-induced neutropenia with fever, high risk, source not yet identified, at the expected nadir after cycle 2 of R-CHOP without growth factor support. Two, anemia and thrombocytopenia from chemotherapy without bleeding. Three, supplement use with a drug interaction concern, since St. John's wort induces CYP3A4 and can lower chemotherapy levels. Four, tobacco use. Five, hypertension with borderline blood pressure in the setting of infection.

Recommendations: Continue cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours and add vancomycin only for instability, port-site infection, or gram-positive cultures. Start filgrastim 480 mcg subcutaneously once daily until the neutrophil count has recovered. Continue acyclovir 400 mg twice daily and ondansetron 8 mg every 8 hours as needed. Hold lisinopril while his blood pressure is low-normal and he is infected. Stop St. John's wort, echinacea, and turmeric capsules now, and no supplements during chemotherapy without oncology review. Start a nicotine patch 21 mg daily and counsel on tobacco cessation. Neutropenic precautions and a daily CBC with differential, with platelet transfusion if below 10 or bleeding, and red cells if hemoglobin falls below 7. For future cycles, give pegfilgrastim 6 mg with each cycle and review chemotherapy dosing with his primary oncologist. We will follow daily.

note:
Nurse: Chart note for the doctor. This is a 63-year-old female here for a three-month follow-up after a pulmonary embolism. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and osteoarthritis of the knees. The allergy list says ibuprofen and naproxen cause hives. Blood pressure 134/80, heart rate 76, oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Doctor: Good morning. It is nice to see you. Last time we talked about the blood clot in your lung. How have you been feeling?

Patient: Better, doctor. I still get a little tired and short of breath when I go up the stairs, but not like before.

Doctor: That can take a while to clear up. Any chest pain, or swelling in your legs?

Patient: No chest pain. No swelling in my legs either.

Doctor: Good. Have you coughed up any blood, or had nosebleeds, bleeding gums, or black stool?

Patient: No, none of that. I get a few bruises on my arms, but they go away.

Doctor: Okay. I want to make sure we get your medicines right. Tell me how you take your blood thinner, the apixaban.

Patient: The pink pill? I take one in the morning, with my breakfast.

Doctor: Just in the morning? Can you read me what the bottle says?

Patient: Let me see. It says five milligrams, take one tablet two times a day. Oh. Two times. I take one in the morning and one at night, yes. My daughter put them in the pill box with two rows. I said it wrong, sorry.

Doctor: That is fine, thank you for checking. So the right way is apixaban 5 mg, one pill morning and one pill night. Can you tell me that back in your own words?

Patient: One pink pill in the morning and one at night, every day. And I do not stop it unless you say.

Doctor: Perfect. What other medicines do you take?

Patient: Lisinopril 10 mg, the one for pressure, once a day. Metformin 500 mg twice a day for the sugar. Atorvastatin 20 mg at night. For my knees I take acetaminophen when needed, 500 mg. And a ginkgo pill from the store for my memory.

Doctor: Thank you. The ginkgo can make you bleed more with the blood thinner, so I would like you to stop it. Do you take any ibuprofen, naproxen, or other anti-inflammatory pain pills?

Patient: No. They gave me hives, so I never take them.

Doctor: Good, please keep avoiding them, because they are also risky with a blood thinner. Now, your blood tests today. Hemoglobin is 13.0, platelets are 250, and creatinine is 0.9, so your kidneys are handling the medicine well. The echocardiogram you had last month showed the right side of your heart is a normal size and the pressure in your lungs is normal. Your blood pressure today is a little high for someone with diabetes, 134 over 80. I would like it under 130 over 80.

Patient: So what do I change?

Doctor: Here is the plan. Number one, keep taking apixaban 5 mg twice a day. At six months we will talk about whether to lower it. Number two, increase your lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg once a day. Number three, stop the ginkgo. Number four, keep the acetaminophen for your knees, but no more than six of the 500 mg pills in one day. Can you tell me what you will change?

Patient: Stop the ginkgo. And take two of my lisinopril pills, the 10 mg ones I have at home, in the morning?

Doctor: Yes, exactly, two of the 10 mg pills once a day makes 20 mg. We will check a basic metabolic panel in two weeks to make sure the lisinopril is agreeing with your kidneys. Call us if you see black stool, blood in your urine, or a nosebleed that lasts more than ten minutes. Call 911 for sudden chest pain or trouble breathing. I will see you again in three months.

Patient: Okay, I understand. Thank you.
summary: A 63-year-old female with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and knee osteoarthritis returned three months after a pulmonary embolism, feeling better but still tired and short of breath on stairs. She denied chest pain, leg swelling, coughing up blood, and nosebleeds. She first described taking apixaban once a day, then read her bottle and confirmed 5 mg twice a day. She has hives with ibuprofen and naproxen. Blood pressure was 134/80, hemoglobin 13.0, and creatinine 0.9. Apixaban 5 mg twice a day was continued, lisinopril was increased to 20 mg once a day, and ginkgo was stopped, with teach-back used throughout.

Doctor: Welcome. I see you are a 19-year-old female here about pelvic pain. Tell me what is going on.

Patient: I have had really bad period pain since I was about fifteen. It keeps getting worse, and now I have pain in my lower belly even on some days when I am not bleeding.

Doctor: How bad is the pain during your period?

Patient: Eight out of ten. I miss one or two days of school every month. It hurts when I have sex, and it hurts when I go to the bathroom during my period.

Doctor: Is there blood in your stool?

Patient: No blood. Just pain.

Doctor: What have you tried?

Patient: Ibuprofen, 600 mg when it starts. It takes the edge off, but I still cannot function. My mom's sister had endometriosis, so I wonder if that is what I have.

Doctor: Any fever, vaginal discharge, burning when you urinate, or weight loss?

Patient: No fever, no discharge, no burning. My weight is the same.

Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 110/68, heart rate 78, and temperature 98.4 F. The urine pregnancy test we did is negative, and the tests for chlamydia and gonorrhea are negative. Your pelvic ultrasound last month was normal, with no cysts. On exam your belly is soft with mild lower abdominal tenderness and no masses. On the pelvic exam, with a chaperone, you had tenderness behind the uterus on the left side, and the uterus moves freely.

Patient: So what does that mean?

Doctor: Based on your story, I think this is most likely endometriosis. A normal ultrasound does not rule it out, because the small spots do not show up on it. We can start treatment without surgery. I want you to start norethindrone acetate 5 mg once a day, taken every day without a break, which should lighten your periods and reduce the pain. I would also like you to switch from ibuprofen to naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food, starting two days before your period and for the first five days of it. Please stop the ibuprofen so you are not taking two anti-inflammatory pills together. A heating pad can help too.

Patient: Okay. What if it does not work?

Doctor: If your pain is not clearly better in three months, we will talk about other hormone options or a small surgery called laparoscopy to look inside and confirm the diagnosis.

Patient: The hard part is I live about two hours away and I do not have a car. I take two buses.

Doctor: I understand. Let us make it easier. We will do your follow-up by video in three months, and I will send a three-month supply of the pills to your pharmacy near home. If your pain suddenly gets much worse, you have a fever, or you faint, go to the nearest emergency room.

Patient: That works. Thank you.
summary: A 19-year-old female reported severe period pain since about age fifteen, now with lower abdominal pain on some non-bleeding days, pain with sex and with bowel movements during her period, and missed school days. She denied blood in her stool, fever, discharge, and burning with urination. Vitals were normal, the urine pregnancy test and chlamydia and gonorrhea tests were negative, and the pelvic ultrasound was normal, with lower abdominal and left posterior pelvic tenderness on exam. The doctor diagnosed likely endometriosis and started norethindrone acetate 5 mg once a day, switching ibuprofen to naproxen. Because she lives far away without a car, follow-up will be by video in three months.
